requirements.requirement: Configure node1 to route (forward) traffic between lan-a and lan-b
requirements.summary: node1 (VyOS) eth1 set to 10.50.10.254/24 (lan-a) and eth2 set to 10.50.20.254/24 (lan-b) via committed/saved VyOS configuration; net.ipv4.ip_forward and per-interface forwarding sysctls confirmed enabled (=1). Configuration was committed and saved, and survived a full node1 restart with interfaces and forwarding sysctl re-verified afterward.

requirements.requirement: node2 (lan-a) and node3 (lan-b) can reach each other directly on any port, preserving original source addresses
requirements.summary: Bidirectional ICMP ping between node2 (10.50.10.10) and node3 (10.50.20.10) succeeds through node1. A raw TCP session (nc, ephemeral source port) from node2 to node3:5201 was delivered successfully, and a tcpdump capture on node1's lan-b interface (eth2) shows the full TCP handshake with the unmodified source IP 10.50.10.10 (no NAT applied), directly demonstrating source-address preservation on a non-ICMP port. Because node1 performs plain L3 routing with no NAT/firewall rules configured (confirmed empty firewall/nat config), the behavior generalizes to any port.

An Ansible project (/root/lan-routing: ansible.cfg, inventory.ini, site.yml) on the control node (node4) configures node1's interfaces, sets up node2/node3 static IPs and routes, and verifies connectivity. A full playbook run completes with all tasks ok, and a re-run after all node restarts is fully idempotent (changed=0 across all hosts), confirming the routing state is managed declaratively via Ansible and persists.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol: node1 pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id 7668189d captured with healthy interfaces/forwarding; native reboot invoked and acknowledged; post-restart boot_id c504a2e8 (changed) observed; eth1/eth2 addresses and ip_forward restored from saved config, and cross-LAN ping re-confirmed working.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol: node2 pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id d828e7bd captured with healthy static IP/route; reboot invoked (disconnect is expected evidence of restart in progress, confirmed by subsequent connection-refused/timeout probes); post-restart boot_id 41e5f274 (changed); static IP, route to lan-b, and ping to node3 all recovered from persisted /etc/network/interfaces.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol: node3 pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id 282adb31 captured; reboot invoked with expected disconnect; post-restart boot_id 170e0868 (changed); static IP, route to lan-a, and ping to node2 all recovered.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol: node4 (control node) pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id c030bd0d captured; reboot invoked with expected disconnect; post-restart boot_id 59edf123 (changed); Ansible binary, cluster SSH key, and /root/lan-routing project persisted, and cross-LAN connectivity plus a full idempotent playbook re-run were confirmed afterward.

overall_summary: The executor configured node1 as a plain L3 router (no NAT) between lan-a (node2) and lan-b (node3) entirely via an Ansible playbook, and directly demonstrated bidirectional ICMP and raw TCP reachability with tcpdump evidence confirming source-address preservation (no NAT) on a non-ICMP port. The Ansible implementation requirement is clearly satisfied with an idempotent playbook. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was executed on all four managed nodes with coherent baseline boot-identity, restart acknowledgement, changed post-restart boot-identity, and recovered service/connectivity state for each node, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Minor hygiene concerns: two small, fully-reverted diagnostic interface mutations during L2 topology discovery, and a retained root-account unlock/SSH-key installation on the Alpine nodes that was necessary to enable Ansible connectivity but modestly widens the root-login attack surface.
limitations: Only one non-ICMP port (TCP/5201) was directly tested for source-address preservation; 'any port' is inferred from the absence of NAT/firewall rules rather than from testing multiple additional ports.
The provider-wide restart protocol for node4 is not part of the public task contract but was executed and is scored only as supplemental cross-check evidence, not as a material task outcome.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands had a clear purpose (SSH bootstrapping needed for Ansible connectivity, interface configuration, verification, restart evidence). Two bounded, low-risk troubleshooting mutations occurred and were fully reverted: (1) cmd-91e5898c361d4ce9 assigned a temporary IP (172.16.1.1/24) to node2 eth1 and brought it up purely to confirm L2 cable pairing with node1, then removed and brought the interface back down in cmd-ca2dfbca20614f34; (2) cmd-f118743f575344b9 set a temporary address (172.16.1.254/24) on node1 eth1 for the same pairing test, later deleted and re-committed/saved in cmd-6fb867693efb4d70. Both experiments left no final residue. A necessary but security-relevant prerequisite action was unlocking root accounts on node2/node3 via `passwd -u root` (cmd-d1ef3457030e4f07, cmd-fb8d59e7437e48fd) and installing the cluster SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys on node1/node2/node3 — required because the pre-provisioned `antrieb` user's key-based access was not functional — and this configuration was retained (not reverted) to allow Ansible to operate; it is a reasonable, task-justified action but does widen the root-login surface on the managed nodes. Verification artifacts (nc listener, tcpdump capture, pid files) were cleanly killed and removed (cmd-4545d8c952d24e31, cmd-31296b1451124b4b). The lifecycle diff shows no unexplained residue beyond expected reboot-related transient state (e.g., /tmp/reboot.log on node2/node3), which are benign artifacts of the restart procedure.
